patterns.title: State/local IT response section order
patterns.guidance: One 2013 US state/local IT winning response (188 pages, about 84,200 words) ordered its sections as: cover letter and bidder forms; a short executive summary first (about 5 pages) making the capability case before any requirement text; the bulk as a point-by-point response in the solicitation's own numbering (about 123 pages, 58% of the response), restating each requirement and answering it in turn; terms and conditions with noted exceptions confined to appendices; a glossary and acronyms at the end; and pricing as a separate cost-schedule attachment, not a narrative section. Use this order only as a starting suggestion for state/local IT proposals; it comes from a single example and does not establish what any other buyer expects.
patterns.locator: Table of Contents; Cover Letter p.1; Executive Summary pp.1-5; Point-by-point response pp.6-136; Appendices A-C

patterns.title: Point-by-point requirements response
patterns.guidance: Answer requirements in the solicitation's own numbering: restate each numbered requirement, then give the response under it. Mark mandatory items explicitly (this solicitation marked them (M) and warned that a 'no' or an omission disqualifies the service from evaluation). Do not build a standalone compliance matrix when the buyer asked for point-by-point answers; this response had no compliance-matrix table and no 'comply' wording. Record any exceptions against the terms and conditions in appendices, not inline in the requirement answers.
patterns.locator: Point-by-point response, pp.6-136; Section 3 mandatory minimums

patterns.title: Short executive summary before the requirement answers
patterns.guidance: Place a short executive summary before the requirement answers (about 5 pages, about 1,300 words in this example): why the bidder, capability and reach, customer satisfaction, market position, research, then a one-paragraph conclusion. Keep terms out of the summary and keep pricing out of the narrative body entirely (terms in appendices, pricing in a separate cost-schedule attachment). Populate every claim from the bidder's own approved evidence; do not import this example's claims, figures or customer references.

records.limitations: One 2013 US state/local IT winning response. The snapshot is a structure-only extraction; the full 188-page PDF is not stored in this repository and its SHA-256 is recorded as documentSha256. The section order does not establish what any other buyer expects. Not a compliance verdict, award evidence for any other procurement, or proof that this structure caused the win.

patterns.title: User-centred prototype approach narrative

Cite the buyer's own playbook or framework where the narrative evidences it, as this submission cited USDS play numbers inline. Do not import this example's user research, personas, team, durations or technology choices; they describe one 2015 prototype, not a current requirement.

patterns.title: Agile delivery approach section order

Use this order only as a starting suggestion for agile delivery responses; it comes from a single 2015 example and its technology choices are historical, not current guidance.

patterns.title: Agile prototype documentation structure
patterns.guidance: Structure prototype documentation as: objective (one sentence stating the decision the prototype supports); collaboration and backlog links; team roles; front-end and back-end sections each with install, run, test and build steps; and a short approach narrative last. Keep installation and deployment instructions separate from the approach narrative so evaluators can run the prototype without reading the rationale first. Do not import this example's team names, tools, hosting choices or URLs.

patterns.title: Iteration-zero discovery before build
patterns.guidance: Begin the approach with an iteration zero: kick-off ideation, target users, a primary use case, an initial feature set and wireframes, before any build. Follow with user research, usability testing, personas and a task flow, then iterative development tracked on a visible board, then a retrospective that feeds a second planning session. End with technical details and installation instructions as separate sections. Do not import this example's team, tools, hosting or usability findings.

patterns.title: Discovery, then daily sprints with usability testing
patterns.guidance: Structure the approach as a dated sequence: ideation (wide net, then top opportunities voted on); discovery (voice of the customer, journey mapping, personas per segment); user stories and wireframes from the core need; a backlog and release plan at the end of day one; then daily sprints with sprint planning, build, usability testing and retrospectives each day. State the testing methods used (this submission named A/B, think-aloud, man-on-the-street and remote tests) and the accessibility standard checked. Do not import this example's personas, stories, test results or technology choices.
patterns.locator: Approach; Get Inspired (Ideation); Start with People (Discovery); Solve for the Core Need; Don't Stop Iterating (Sprint); Conclusion
